newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar counted match-fixing payoff, court told.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar counted match-fixing payoff, court told.

text.p: Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar got 40,000 pounds ($67,000) for rigging a match but missed out on larger payouts by making inadvertant saves in later games, a court heard on Monday.

Chris Vincent, chief prosecution witness in a match-fixing trial against Grobbelaar and three others, said the keeper threw the game against Newcastle for a Far Eastern betting syndicate in late November 1993.
Grobbelaar is accused of fixing matches with the help of former striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessmen Heng Suan Lim, who both received large cash sums from the Far East.
The prosecution says Lim -- dubbed the "Short Man" by Grobbelaar -- and Fashanu were middlemen. Neither could explain where the money had come from.
Vincent said that shortly after the Newcastle game, which Liverpool lost 3-0, he and Grobbelaar had flown to London and then driven to a mansion in a northern suburb.
"On the way there Grobbelaar told me we were going to pick up 40,000 pounds," said Vincent, a former business partner of Grobbelaar until the two men fell out in June 1994.

Grobbelaar, carrying a briefcase, was met at the front door by Fashanu and went inside. A few minutes later he reappeared, got into the car and told Vincent to retrieve a brown envelope from the case and count the money inside.

"I counted out the money -- it was all in 50 pound notes. It came to 40,000 pounds and I confirmed to Grobbelaar that there was 40,000 pounds there," said Vincent, who like Grobbelaar is from Zimbabwe.
"Grobbelaar told me Fashanu had made between 400,000 and 800,000 pounds doing business with the Short Man," he added. The prosecution says Grobbelaar tried to rig four games.
The court was later played excerpts from video tapes of conversations between the two men which Vincent covertly recorded with the aid of the Sun tabloid newspaper.
Grobbelaar could be heard lamenting that he lost a payout of 125,000 pounds by accidentally making a save in a game against Manchester United in January 1994 that ended in a 3-3 draw.
"In the second half I made two blinding saves, but I was diving the wrong way," said the keeper. "I dived the wrong way and went "Phew' and it hit my hand."
There was also an away game against Norwich in February 1994 which he told the Short Man that Liverpool would lose.
But it ended in a 2-2 draw, partly because Grobbelaar deflected a shot with his legs. After the game he discovered 15 messages waiting on his mobile phone.
"I'm telling you that's the Short Man and he's going to be as mad as a snake," Vincent quoted Grobbelaar as saying.
Vincent, awaiting trial for perverting the course of justice, said Grobbelaar decided to fix games because he was unhappy at being paid less than others in the Liverpool team.

The partnership between the two men ended in June 1994 when Grobbelaar resigned as a director of a firm Vincent had set up to promote safari tours to Zimbabwe. The bust-up followed disputes over a safari park the firm wanted to lease.

"That was the end of the project, of the friendship, of everything," said Vincent. A month later he contacted the Sun and agreed he would approach Grobbelaar pretending to represent another betting syndicate that wanted matches rigged.
The other man on trial is former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, accused with Lim and Fashanu of taking part in a separate bid to fix matches. All four pleaded not guilty.
